questions.question: A Pushdown Automaton (PDA) is formally defined as a tuple with how many components?
In the PDA tuple (Q, Σ, Γ, δ, q0, Z0, F), Γ represents:

options.A: The set of input symbols
options.B: The set of stack symbols
options.C: The set of final states
options.D: The transition function

questions.question: In the PDA tuple, Z0 represents:

options.A: The initial state
options.B: The final state
options.C: The initial stack symbol
options.D: The blank symbol

questions.question: What is the key extra memory component that distinguishes a PDA from a finite automaton?

options.A: A read-only input tape
options.B: An auxiliary stack (LIFO memory)
options.C: A second finite state set
options.D: An infinite tape

questions.question: The transition function δ of a PDA has the general form:

options.B: δ: Q × Σ → Q
options.C: δ: Γ → Q
options.D: δ: Q × Γ → Σ

questions.question: An Instantaneous Description (ID) of a PDA is typically written as:

options.A: (q, w, γ) — current state, remaining input, stack contents
options.B: (q, w) only
options.C: (w, γ) only
options.D: (q, F) — state and final states

questions.question: The 'turnstile' notation ⊢ in PDA IDs represents:

options.A: Equality of two IDs
options.B: A single move (one transition) from one ID to another
options.C: The final accepting state
options.D: The empty stack

questions.question: Acceptance of a string 'by final state' means:

options.A: The PDA reaches a state in F with the stack necessarily empty
options.B: The PDA reaches a state in F after consuming the entire input, regardless of remaining stack content
options.C: The stack must contain only Z0
options.D: The PDA halts with no moves left, regardless of state

questions.question: Acceptance of a string 'by empty stack' means:

options.A: The PDA's stack becomes completely empty after reading the entire input, regardless of the current state
options.B: The PDA must be in a final state with an empty stack
options.C: The stack must contain exactly Z0
options.D: The input must be empty

questions.question: For acceptance by final state, the language is defined as:

options.D: L(M) = { w | stack is empty at the end }

questions.question: For acceptance by empty stack, the language is defined as:

options.A: N(M) = { w | (q0, w, Z0) ⊢* (q, ε, ε), for any state q }
options.C: N(M) requires q ∈ F strictly
options.D: N(M) is always equal to L(M)

questions.question: A PDA is called deterministic (DPDA) if:

options.A: It has more than one start state
options.B: For every (state, input symbol or ε, stack top), δ gives at most one possible move, with restrictions on ε-moves
options.C: It never uses a stack
options.D: Every string is accepted

questions.question: Which class of languages do deterministic PDAs accept (by final state)?

options.A: All context-free languages
options.B: Deterministic Context-Free Languages (DCFLs), a proper subset of CFLs
options.C: Only regular languages
options.D: Only context-sensitive languages

questions.question: Is the language {aⁿbⁿ | n ≥ 1} deterministic context-free?

options.A: No, it requires nondeterminism
options.B: Yes, it can be accepted by a DPDA
options.C: It is not context-free at all
options.D: It is regular, not context-free

questions.question: Is the language of palindromes over {a,b} (odd or even length) deterministic context-free?

options.A: Yes, always deterministic
options.B: No, it generally requires a nondeterministic PDA (the 'middle' of the string can't be detected deterministically without a center marker)
options.C: It is regular
options.D: It cannot be accepted by any PDA

questions.question: Every language accepted by a PDA using acceptance-by-empty-stack:

options.A: Is always regular
options.B: Is also acceptable by some PDA using acceptance-by-final-state, and vice versa
options.C: Can never be accepted by final state
options.D: Is never context-free

questions.question: To convert a PDA accepting by empty stack (N(M)) into one accepting by final state (L(M')), the standard construction:

options.A: Removes the stack entirely
options.B: Adds a new initial state and a new final state, with an ε-transition on seeing the original start symbol under the new bottom marker
options.C: Simply relabels all states as final
options.D: Requires no change at all

questions.question: To convert a PDA accepting by final state (L(M)) into one accepting by empty stack (N(M')), the standard construction:

options.A: Adds a new state that, upon reaching any final state of M, pops all remaining stack symbols via ε-moves
options.B: Deletes all final states
options.C: Requires the original stack alphabet to be regular
options.D: Cannot be done in general

questions.question: In a PDA, an ε-move refers to a transition where:

options.A: The input symbol is ignored (no input is consumed)
options.B: The stack is always popped
options.C: The state never changes
options.D: The input must be exactly ε

questions.question: A PDA can be thought of as an NFA equipped with:

options.A: A second input tape
options.B: An additional stack for auxiliary storage
options.C: Two-way input head movement
options.D: A read/write tape like a Turing Machine

questions.question: The class of languages accepted by PDAs is exactly:

options.A: Regular languages
options.B: Context-Free Languages (CFLs)
options.C: Context-Sensitive Languages
options.D: Recursively Enumerable Languages

options.A: The new ID is (p, w, βγ'γ)

questions.question: In PDA notation, if δ(q, ε, Z) is defined, this move:

options.A: Requires an input symbol to be present
options.B: Can be taken without consuming any input symbol
options.C: Always leads to rejection
options.D: Only applies at the start state

options.A: Final-state acceptance ignores the stack content once a final state is reached after consuming input
options.B: The stack must always be empty by definition
options.C: This situation never occurs
options.D: Final state and empty stack are always synonymous

questions.question: For empty-stack acceptance N(M), the set of final states F is:

options.A: Required to be all states of Q
options.B: Irrelevant / typically not needed at all (can be defined as F = ∅)
options.C: Always a singleton set
options.D: Must equal Q − {q0}

questions.question: For a DPDA, which condition is required regarding ε-moves and regular moves from the same configuration?

options.A: Both an ε-move and an a-move can be enabled simultaneously
options.B: If an ε-move is defined for (q, ε, Z), no a-move (a ∈ Σ) can also be defined for (q, a, Z)
options.C: ε-moves are forbidden entirely in a DPDA

questions.question: Which of the following languages is NOT deterministic context-free (though it is context-free)?

options.A: {aⁿbⁿ | n ≥ 1}
options.B: { w wᴿ | w ∈ {a,b}* } (even-length palindromes without a center marker)
options.C: {aⁿbᵐ | n,m ≥ 0}

questions.question: The class DCFL (deterministic context-free languages) is:

options.A: Exactly equal to the class of CFLs
options.B: A strict (proper) subset of CFLs
options.C: A superset of CFLs
options.D: Equal to the regular languages

options.B: DCFLs are closed under union
options.C: DCFLs are closed under intersection with regular languages
options.D: DCFLs are closed under reversal

questions.question: The equivalence proof that acceptance by empty stack and acceptance by final state accept the same class of languages shows:

options.B: Because q0 cannot be reused in any PDA
options.C: To increase the input alphabet size
options.D: There is no real reason; it's optional

options.A: To prevent the new 'stack emptying' state from being triggered while symbols under the original Z0 still remain, avoiding accidental premature acceptance
options.B: Because the original Z0 is deleted
options.C: It is never needed
options.D: To make M′ nondeterministic

questions.question: A PDA can be used to construct a CFG such that both generate/accept exactly the same language. This shows:

options.A: PDAs are strictly weaker than CFGs
options.B: PDAs and CFGs are equivalent in expressive power
options.C: CFGs cannot express what PDAs accept

questions.question: In the standard CFG-to-PDA construction (via GNF), the PDA typically has:

options.A: Many states, one per non-terminal
options.B: Just a single state, with transitions derived directly from each GNF production
options.C: No stack at all

questions.question: In the CFG-to-PDA construction, the stack of the PDA is used to simulate:

options.A: The remaining unread input
options.B: The current sentential form (specifically, the leftmost pending non-terminals)
options.C: The set of final states

options.A: Single letters only, unrelated to PDA states
options.B: [q, A, p] representing 'starting in state q with A on top of stack, we can empty A and reach state p'

questions.question: Which of the following is a valid application of PDAs?

options.A: Matching balanced parentheses in expressions
options.B: Recognizing arbitrary context-sensitive constraints requiring more than a stack
options.C: Performing arithmetic multiplication directly
options.D: Sorting an array of numbers

questions.question: Which statement about the power of PDAs versus Turing Machines is correct?

options.A: PDAs are strictly more powerful than Turing Machines
options.B: PDAs are strictly less powerful than Turing Machines (PDAs cannot recognize all recursively enumerable/context-sensitive languages)

options.B: It reads input right to left only

options.A: Accepted regardless

options.B: Pushes one symbol (e.g., X) onto the stack for each 'a' read

options.B: Pop one X from the stack (matching the count of a's)

questions.question: Which statement about PDA equivalence to CFGs is FALSE?

options.A: Every CFG has an equivalent PDA that accepts the same language
options.B: Every PDA has an equivalent CFG that generates the same language
options.C: PDAs can only simulate regular grammars, not full CFGs
options.D: Both directions of conversion (CFG→PDA and PDA→CFG) are constructive/algorithmic

questions.question: A PDA is used to accept L(G) for some CFG G. What determines when the PDA finishes successfully (informally)?

options.A: When all input is read and the simulated derivation (stack) has been fully resolved into the input string (commonly represented by an empty stack)
options.B: When the PDA reads exactly one symbol
options.C: When the stack reaches its maximum possible size
options.D: PDAs cannot represent CFG derivations at all

questions.question: Which of these grammars would generally require a PDA with more elaborate stack manipulation to accept its language?

options.A: A regular grammar (already acceptable via FA-style logic with a trivial stack)
options.B: A deeply nested, recursive CFG such as one for balanced/matched bracket structures at arbitrary depth
options.C: A grammar with no productions at all
options.D: A grammar generating only the empty string

questions.question: For the PDA-to-CFG construction, why is the resulting grammar guaranteed to be context-free?

options.A: Because each derived production has exactly one non-terminal on the left (the triple [q,A,p]) by construction
options.B: Because all PDAs are regular by definition
options.C: Because the PDA's stack alphabet is always empty
options.D: It is not guaranteed; the resulting grammar could be context-sensitive

questions.question: Which of the following is an accurate way to think about a PDA versus an NFA in terms of raw computational model?

options.A: A PDA = NFA + an unbounded stack
options.B: A PDA = DFA + a second finite-state control
options.C: A PDA = NFA − states
options.D: A PDA = Turing Machine − stack

questions.question: Which languages can be recognized by a PDA that never actually uses (pushes/pops meaningfully onto) its stack?

options.A: Only context-sensitive languages
options.B: Exactly the regular languages (since ignoring the stack reduces the PDA to behaving like an NFA)
options.C: No languages at all
options.D: Only languages with a single string

questions.question: Why does a PDA's stack need to be, in principle, of unbounded size (not fixed)?

options.A: Because CFLs like aⁿbⁿ require counting an arbitrarily large, unbounded n, which a fixed-size memory cannot track
options.B: Because the input alphabet is always infinite
options.C: Because states must be counted somewhere
options.D: A bounded stack would work fine for all CFLs

questions.question: Which of these is a correct general statement about equivalence of PDA acceptance criteria and grammar ambiguity?

options.A: An ambiguous CFG always leads to a PDA that rejects all strings
options.B: PDA acceptance (empty-stack or final-state) doesn't directly resolve grammar ambiguity — a PDA built from an ambiguous CFG may still have multiple accepting computation paths for the same string
options.C: PDAs automatically disambiguate any CFG
options.D: Ambiguity is irrelevant to any PDA construction

questions.question: Which best describes why the study of PDAs is placed right after the study of CFGs in a Theory of Computation course?

options.A: Because PDAs and CFGs are unrelated and studied independently
options.B: Because PDAs provide the automaton-theoretic (recognition) counterpart to CFGs' generative definition of context-free languages
options.C: Because PDAs are a simplification of finite automata only
options.D: Because PDAs replace the need to study CFGs at all

questions.question: Which of the following would be the most direct real-world use of PDA theory in software engineering?

options.A: Implementing syntax checking/parsing for nested structures like XML tags, JSON braces, or programming-language blocks
options.B: Sorting large datasets efficiently
options.C: Performing floating-point arithmetic
options.D: Managing network routing tables

questions.question: Which statement correctly relates PDAs to the pumping lemma for context-free languages?

options.A: PDAs are unrelated to any pumping-style argument
options.B: Since a PDA's stack has a bound tied to the number of states/stack symbols for 'short' computations, sufficiently long accepted strings force a stack-height repetition, which underlies the CFL pumping lemma
options.C: The pumping lemma only applies to regular languages recognized by PDAs
options.D: PDAs disprove the pumping lemma for CFLs

questions.question: In the formal PDA tuple, Σ represents:

options.A: The stack alphabet
options.B: The finite set of input symbols
options.C: The set of final states
options.D: The transition function

questions.question: Which of the following is true about the initial stack symbol Z0?

options.A: Z0 must always be a member of the input alphabet Σ
options.B: Z0 ∈ Γ, and the stack initially contains only Z0 before any input is processed
options.C: Z0 is always equal to the start state q0
options.D: Z0 is optional and can be omitted from the PDA definition

questions.question: Which best defines the term 'Instantaneous Description' (ID) for a PDA?

options.A: A snapshot capturing the current state, remaining input, and current stack content at some point during computation
options.B: Only the current state of the PDA
options.C: A description of the PDA's transition function in full
options.D: The final accepted string only

questions.question: Which move type in a PDA does NOT consume any input symbol?

options.A: A move using δ(q,a,X) for a ∈ Σ
options.B: A move using δ(q,ε,X)
options.C: Both types always consume input
options.D: Neither type is valid in a PDA

questions.question: For acceptance 'by final state', is it required that the stack be empty when the input is fully consumed?

options.A: Yes, strictly required
options.B: No — only reaching a state in F after consuming all input matters; the stack can be non-empty
options.C: Only if F contains exactly one state
options.D: Only for deterministic PDAs

questions.question: For acceptance 'by empty stack', is it required that the ending state be in F?

options.A: Yes, always
options.B: No — the state at the end is irrelevant; only the stack being empty matters
options.C: Only for deterministic PDAs
options.D: Only if the input string has even length

questions.question: A DPDA differs from an NPDA primarily in that:

options.A: A DPDA can have multiple valid transitions per configuration, while NPDA cannot
options.B: A DPDA has at most one valid transition per configuration (with ε-move restrictions), while an NPDA may have several
options.C: DPDAs never use a stack
options.D: NPDAs cannot accept any language a DPDA accepts

questions.question: Is {aⁿbⁿ | n ≥ 1} a Deterministic Context-Free Language (DCFL)?

options.A: No, it requires nondeterminism
options.B: Yes; a simple deterministic PDA (push on a, pop on b) suffices
options.C: It's not even context-free
options.D: It's regular, so the question doesn't apply

questions.question: Which of the following best distinguishes CFL from DCFL?

options.A: CFL is a strict superset of DCFL — every DCFL is context-free, but some CFLs (needing guesswork/nondeterminism) are not deterministic
options.B: DCFL is a strict superset of CFL
options.C: CFL and DCFL are always identical
options.D: Neither class contains the other

questions.question: The theorem proving that empty-stack acceptance and final-state acceptance define the same class of languages requires:

options.A: Only one direction of construction (empty-stack to final-state)
options.B: Two separate constructions: one converting empty-stack PDAs to final-state PDAs, and one converting final-state PDAs to empty-stack PDAs
options.C: No construction; it's assumed without proof
options.D: Rewriting the PDA as a CFG first

questions.question: In the empty-stack-to-final-state conversion, once the simulated original PDA's stack is 'emptied' (exposing the new bottom marker), the new machine:

options.A: Rejects immediately
options.B: Takes an ε-move into a new, dedicated final state to signal acceptance
options.C: Restarts the computation from q0
options.D: Ignores this event entirely

questions.question: In the final-state-to-empty-stack conversion, what happens to the original stack alphabet symbols once a final state of M is reached?

options.A: They remain forever on the stack, and the string is rejected
options.B: They are systematically popped via added ε-transitions in the new machine, until the stack is empty
options.C: They are converted into input symbols
options.D: Nothing changes; only the state matters

questions.question: Which of the following correctly restates the CFG-PDA equivalence theorem?

options.A: A language L is context-free if and only if there exists some PDA M such that L = L(M) (or equivalently N(M))
options.B: A language L is context-free if and only if it is accepted by some DFA
options.C: A language L is regular if and only if some PDA accepts it
options.D: PDAs can only accept finite languages, unlike CFGs

questions.question: When building a PDA from a CFG via the GNF-based method, what happens if the grammar contains a production A → a (no non-terminals following)?

options.A: The PDA reads a, pops A, and pushes nothing (an empty string) back onto the stack
options.B: The PDA cannot handle this case at all
options.C: The PDA pushes A back onto the stack unchanged
options.D: This production is simply ignored

questions.question: In the PDA-to-CFG construction, why must every PDA move be systematically translated into one or more grammar productions?

options.A: To ensure the resulting grammar's derivations exactly correspond to the PDA's accepting computations
options.B: Because grammars have no relation to PDA moves
options.C: To make the grammar regular
options.D: Because otherwise the PDA cannot be simulated by any grammar

questions.question: Which best describes an intuitive real-world analogy for a PDA's stack?

options.A: A queue of tasks processed first-in-first-out
options.B: A stack of plates, where only the top plate can be added or removed (last-in-first-out)
options.C: A random-access array with direct indexing
options.D: A circular buffer with fixed size

questions.question: Which of these correctly completes: 'A PDA accepts by empty stack if, after reading the entire input, ___ .'

options.A: it is in a final state, regardless of stack content
options.B: the stack contains only Z0
options.C: the stack contains no symbols at all
options.D: the input pointer resets to the beginning

questions.question: Which best explains why real compilers rarely use raw nondeterministic PDAs directly for parsing?

options.A: Nondeterministic simulation can be computationally expensive; deterministic (or near-deterministic) parsing techniques (like LL/LR, based on DPDA-like behavior) are preferred for efficiency
options.B: PDAs cannot represent programming language syntax at all
options.C: Compilers never use any automaton-based theory
options.D: NPDAs always reject valid programs

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of a context-free (but not regular) language recognizable by a PDA?

options.A: { w ∈ {a,b}* | w contains an even number of a's }
options.B: { aⁿbⁿ | n ≥ 0 }
options.D: { w | w starts with a }

questions.question: Overall, what is the central theoretical contribution of Unit 4 (Pushdown Automata) in a Theory of Computation course?

options.A: Establishing the automaton model (PDA) that exactly recognizes context-free languages, complementing the generative model (CFG) studied earlier, and covering both acceptance modes, determinism, and CFG-PDA equivalence
options.B: Proving that all languages are regular
options.C: Introducing Turing Machines for the first time
options.D: Showing that context-free languages don't exist
